Mike Davis

Mike Davis has fashioned a robust career as a trombonist, composer, arranger, and music educator. His history of gigs and accomplishments include tours with the Rolling Stones, sessions with Bob Dylan, and concerts with his own Hip- Bone Big Band.
Mike was interviewed via Zoom on April 1, 2024 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe, I’m very pleased to have Mike Davis with me for the Fillius Jazz Archive. Welcome, sir.
Good to be with you, Monk. Thanks so much for having me.
Right off the top of the bat, would you define “freelance” as in freelance musician?

That’s a great question. I mean I think of a freelance player as somebody who basically has the ability and the range stylistically and do a lot of, a wide variety of work. And I think if that’s not the definition that would certainly be a helpful quality if you’re going to be a freelance player. And I guess to a certain degree freelance implies that you’re not holding down a steady, full time job I suppose. But a freelance player to me is everybody outside of say somebody who has an orchestral job or somebody who has a professorship at a university or college, and people who just aren’t relying on one single thing to make a living as a musician.
That sort of defines what your career has been. Would you agree with that?
I totally agree with that. Absolutely.
Yeah. What have you done over the years to make sure that you never miss a gig?

Well it’s — I’ll tell ya, first of all I’m a nervous, paranoid wreck. I’m originally from California but I’ve been in New York so long that I’m, you know, the classic paranoid New Yorker. So I’m always, I’m habitually early — like really early. So you know I always say I’d rather be two hours early to a gig than be five minutes late. So there’s that part of it, and then I actually keep an old-fashioned date book that I write in by hand and that’s the only thing I really feel comfortable doing. I get made fun of by my sons and rightfully so, I should kind of jump into the — maybe even jump into the twentieth century, then we can go to the twenty-first century. But yeah I try to be pretty meticulous about it and I’ve never — I haven’t been late or missed a gig so far but I’ll knock on wood because sure enough tomorrow you know, something bad happens on the George Washington Bridge and I don’t get in.

I’m going to pause for one second to turn off a fan. Yes I have a refrigerator calendar and a paper calendar, and every few days I like set them next to one another ‘cause I just — I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
think three times in my career I’ve done that, missed something, and boy that is a bad feeling.
Oh it’s terri- yeah. It’s not where you want to be, that’s for sure.

I’m wondering, about the time you were at Eastman and looking at it as a career, did you have this urge to do multiple things in the music business? Or was it a practical decision that came as it went along? Like opportunities came up and you said well I bet I can do this? How calculated was it?

Yeah that’s another great question, Monk. I think it was pretty calculated. I had a jazz background as a kid, my dad was a jazz educator at a community college out in California. So I was around it a lot and I played piano and I played drums before I got to the trombone. And you know I always just kind of wanted to be able to make a living as an instrumentalist even though my passion was certainly jazz. But you know my degree from Eastman was in classical trombone but that was back in the day when they didn’t have an undergraduate jazz major. But I got a lot out of that. That was a tremendously helpful degree. And you know to be quite honest, Monk, my main goal was to become a studio musician and so people like Bill Reichenbach and Chuck Findley and Urbie Green and, you know, scores of others but those come to mind right away. You know I looked at all of them and they were a generation or sometimes two generations ahead of me, and I just noticed how versatile they were and how they could be put into any situation and be able to function at a high level. So I really kind of wanted to do that and then obviously play jazz as well. And because I had the classical background from Eastman, you know I started getting calls to do movie sessions and things of that nature, which are more — lend themselves more generally speaking to a classical approach but with pop sensibility to your approach. But anyway I kind of always was looking at doing a variety of things and I really liked that and I think trying to model myself after those studio musicians, it was kind of incumbent on me to be able to do different — stylistically do different things. So it kind of was — in a way it was calculated but in a way it was natural because that’s kind of what I was trying to do.
You’re expected to play the part basically correct the first time. Is that true?

I would say it’s partially true. I mean I think it’s different for different types of things. Like for instance if you’re playing in a large orchestra for a film score, the chances of them taking the first take are very low because there’s microphone issues, there’s maybe some copying issues in the parts, there’s balance issues that they want to go back and check. So you will have an opportunity to get a take or two, and I think, you know certainly in big band recording stuff, all kinds of other, TV commercials which used to be a big thing in New York, typically they don’t take the first take, but you want to certainly be in the ballpark for sure. But I think it’s much different for, especially a small group © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

type of jazz recording for sure, then you want to be on your game as much as you can be on that first take because that might have a vibe that really lends itself to, you know, the music being served as best as possible and you might get something that you don’t get in subsequent takes. I know in producing my own records, and we just did a new big band record last year. And you know I’m not sure we kept — of the ten tracks there might have been one that was a first take but most of them were second or third takes. But then after that I find it gets to diminishing returns and then you’re kind of like oh wow this wasn’t as good and then now it’s a little bit dangerous when you’re producing it like when do you call it and say okay we can work with this and let’s stay with this one. But that’s what these really good producers have figured out — how to you know, not go over the cliff and start getting diminishing returns.
This morning I was watching your video of “Open City.”
Yeah, yeah.
It just sounded fantastic. The recording quality and the playing, the whole package. Do you recall how many takes that one took?

I do actually. Thank you for mentioning that track. I’m super fond of it and it was actually a composition/arrangement by my son, Cole Davis, who is an outstanding bass player and writer as well. And that was three takes. We did three takes on that. And all three of them were usable. In fact sometimes we’ll use a little bit — oh you know what? I like this solo from that take so let’s like move — you know you can, the technology is at such a high level nowadays, there’s a lot of — you know editing is the best word for it. There’s a lot of editing you can do with a good engineer. But for instance the two soloists on that were Troy Roberts on tenor saxophone and Mike Rodriguez who is one of my favorite trumpet players on trumpet. And all three of their solos it was just like what do you want? Do you want a ten or a ten or a ten? Which one would you like? So those guys make it so easy and everybody played so great. And I have to mention that our drummer, Jared Schonig really just played so beautifully on the whole record but on that track in particular. Overall we went with Take #3 on that.
Yeah your drummer had a — he has a great expression on his face when he gets through it.

He is so fun to watch and he’s like I can’t watch him when my band’s playing ‘cause I’m sitting next to him. And so he’s really passionate about his playing and puts — I mean you know strangely enough Monk, he was really really sick at those recording sessions. He had gotten a stomach bug and it was questionable whether he was able to do it. And we brought in a bunch of hydration drinks and stuff for him and he would just lay down in between takes and — but you’d have no idea by the way he played. So much energy and passion in his approach. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

I want to try a little experiment that I don’t think I’ve ever done this in an interview, but one thing I liked about that track and some others I listened to of yours is that they have something that’s memorable when it’s over. And you can sing it back in your head. So if someone asked you “Oh yeah, what’s that thing ‘Open City’ you did, how does that go again?” How would you verbalize something from the tune?
Yeah.
What would you verbalize?
I’m not a good singer so I won’t sing.
Well go ahead ‘cause I’m not either.

I mean I could, in a really horrific way sing the melody that Cole wrote, but yeah I think I would probably say that I — in my own writing and I think Cole does the same thing — we really like to have some level of accessibility to it so that it feels like, you know, what you just described, and I really appreciate that, because that’s definitely something we’re going for. And I kind of learned that from my years of a couple of decades of being in Bob Mintzer’s band and I’ve always been a huge Bob fan and I’m so thrilled I got to work for him for so long before he moved to Los Angeles. But to me his music really had that kind of quality. There was always something that I would take away in kind of a memorable way like you just described. So I suppose part of that comes from emulating Bob a little bit.

I wrote down a note here saying it must be a luxury to write for players like that who are going to play it so wonderfully. And then I realized that it’s a luxury that you may have to pay for yourself.

That’s a hundred percent accurate. Yes. Yeah, it’s not — to make a big band record you’re really not looking to recoup even a modest amount of your investment in the product itself. Yes. You’re absolutely right. It’s absolutely fantastic to work with musicians of the caliber on “Open City” is and you know there’s so many really stand out excellent players in New York so we always talk about the depth of players here. So you get down to your eighth call trombone player, it’s still going to be really good. As opposed to some cities that could have — all cities have really good players no doubt, but it’s the depth that you don’t really have so much of. So that’s a real plus here in New York being able to just — and I was able to get pretty much — all my first call people were available. And I booked it for the beginning of January which is typically like a little bit slower timeframe. So if I were trying to book it like for right now, the spring or summer, it would be hit and miss in terms of the players. But yes, it’s a very expensive proposition to do it. And I try to make sure everybody gets paid. I would love to be able to pay them more but I think I’ve built a reputation of being fair and trying to be as © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
generous as I can. But you’re a hundred percent right, you are going to pay for that if you decide to do that project.

So among your projects, you’ve had “Trumpets 11,” you’ve had a project with seemingly every trombone player in New York in “Brass Nation,” 55 of the world’s finest brass players. So don’t you think you ought to try some big project now? I had a situation — some years ago I did my own record and I had Bill Watrous and Jerome Richardson on it. I had this weird feeling, like on a couple of occasions they weren’t exactly playing what I had written sort of exactly like I wanted it. But I had a hard time telling those guys like anything. Have you had that circumstance with all these — you’ve bad Bobby Shew and Chuck Findley and —

Oh without question. And I think, you know, undoubtedly you approached it in a similar way. Like I just try to be — I try to express what I’m thinking and what I want to be different but I do it in a very respectful and nice, hopefully nice way. But I’m certainly, and I was fortunate to work with Bill Watrous myself quite a bit and, you know, especially people of my generation, Bill was a big time hero and you know, you just kind of naturally react to that. But there were a couple of times with Bill like when we were recording the “Absolute Trombone” record where he kind of didn’t want to do it the way I wanted him to do it. I kind of just was like all right, you’re Bill Watrous, you do it the way you want. But for the most part it rarely ends up being that.
Is there — with technology these days — is there a feeling sometimes that you’re giving it away for free?

For sure, yeah. It is very challenging and if I were doing a project like “Open City” like I said for the money or in the hopes of recouping the investment in it, it would be foolhardy. There is, you know the old time go down to Tower Records and spend $8 or $10 on a record and that’s it and you know, people can make bootleg cassettes or whatever. But now I mean pretty much as soon as the record comes out it’s on YouTube for free. So you know I think there are people who — I’m certainly one of them — that when I — I want to buy the music because I want to support the artist that I’m getting so much joy and enjoyment out of listening to. So to me I think there are a lot of people like that but then I think there are a lot of people that — especially in the younger generation, in fairness to them, you know they’re used to getting everything for free in terms of their music, or at a very low cost. So these streaming services like Apple or Spotify, whatever, the amount, it’s fractions of a penny every time it gets played. So there’s little hope of making much other than pocket change back from that side of things. You know I have my own company, Hip-Bone Music and so we’ll sell the arrangements through that so that’s a possible revenue stream in terms of recouping. It still won’t get anywhere near your initial investment. But I think you look at it in the sense that it’s an expensive © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

calling card. Or business card. It’s saying here’s my new stuff that I’ve been working on and hopefully the byproduct is some gigs you weren’t expecting maybe or appearances at a college or a high school that wants to hire you as a guest, those type of things. And I do think that that is a lane that you can get in and have some success with that. But again you’re still — you have to make an initial investment that probably won’t be recouped.
Musicians are going to do it anyway, aren’t they?

Absolutely. Absolutely. Yeah I mean it’s actually quite amazing to me how many big bands are going right now in New York over the last couple years. Big band leaders, younger players all the way up to folks my age and ten, fifteen years older than me. Yeah. I mean they keep coming, they keep doing it, and it’s great. It’s great. Because that’s what it is — it is about the music and it is about serving the music and getting it out there. So I think it’s great that people are passionate about their music and their projects and it’s important. But you’re right, the musicians are going to keep doing that regardless of the shortfall in terms of the economics.
I watched a video of you playing “Waiting on a Friend” at the Burghausen Fest, and I will have to say that’s an impressive display of sackbut ability.
Well you’re very kind Monk, thank you. Yeah some days I feel like I can get around the thing and other days I’m trying to figure it out still.

Well that leads me to — what are you — let’s put it this way, if you met somebody who is not a musician, like my father used to be so confused by what are they doing. He’d hear somebody that was clearly improvising and I couldn’t — at the time I can’t remember what I said to him. But can you succinctly explain to someone just a kernel of what improvising is?

I probably won’t be very succinct but I’ll try anyway. Yeah I think of it as you know the thing I would draw the closest parallel to might be if you listen to a Mozart symphony you’re going to hear melody, you’re going to hear harmony, and then you’re going to hear counterpoint, which is material that is supplementing and complementing the melody and the harmony. And that’s all written down in an orchestral composition. But to me, you know we talked about Charlie Parker earlier. Charlie Parker, his improvisation is basically the same as Mozart counterpoint except that he’s doing it on the fly. He’s not writing it down, he’s not — he hasn’t necessarily prepared it although I think jazz musicians develop a vocabulary that they’re comfortable using. That’s why any of us can hear Charlie Parker and know right away it’s Charlie Parker. Or you can hear right away that it’s Mike Rodriguez or pick whoever you like. So to me I guess I’ve already crossed the line of being succinct but to me it’s really, it’s counterpoint. It’s that element of the music that you’re used to hearing in a symphony or in anything — in rock & roll too. Maybe they wouldn’t break it down in the same way but there’s kind of those three or © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

four elements and the one element in jazz that is counterpoint is an improvised solo that’s happening in real time. You’re not writing down anything, you’re not playing exactly what you prepared, you’re reacting to the other players and the other input you’re getting from the other players as opposed to a written symphony. But conceptually it’s kind of the same kind of material.

That particular song I mentioned, that Stones song, has a fairly basic chord progression. Do you feel that you’re more likely to play outside the changes on a song like that, that has less harmonic material than I guess — more than what — well maybe like a standard bebop with more changes.

I think the answer to that would be yes for me. I mean I think it’s easier — easier is not the right word — I think it lends itself to more harmonic experimentation if the bass of the chords, the harmonic movement of the chords, is simpler. It gives you I think a little bit more time to develop things in terms of playing outside the key centers. But that said of course you can listen to, you know pick whoever you want but you know you listen to John Coltrane play, he’s using all kinds of substitutions on standards and chords, tritone substitutions, all kinds of different — and superimposing different chords over the top of another chord. So I think it’s still very — it lends itself very much so to reharmonizing, even when there’s more harmonic movement and more kind of — what’s the right word — complex chord changes. Let’s say that.
Is there such a thing as wrong notes for you?
Yeah.
Me too.

Yeah I mean you know certainly playing — I mean for a brass player it’s kind of interesting. This was my first job when I got out of college was with Buddy Rich, which I’m still to this day grateful for that opportunity. It was awesome. He, you know he was a lunatic in his own kind of way but a genius in another way. And I was so thrilled to get the call on that. I actually left Eastman three months before graduation, much to the chagrin of my mom and everybody else that, “You’re making a mistake.” I knew I wasn’t, and I didn’t. It was a good move and I got to play with Buddy for two years and got tremendous growth out of it, it’s probably that. But Buddy would always scream and yell whenever brass players would crack a note. So when we crack a note it’s just when somehow our embouchure doesn’t respond in the way we want it to. To me that’s different from a wrong note. A wrong note is playing, “Oh I was supposed to play a B natural there but I played a B flat instead.” Okay that’s a wrong note to me. But that’s a brass player thing. So we kind of have to deal with trumpet and trombone and tuba and French horn — we have to kind of deal with that aspect of instrumental playing that other, you know a piano player wouldn’t have to deal with something like that, or a guitar © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

player. But certainly in terms of improvisation if I play a note that’s — I’m not intending, and I can’t figure out my way to get out of it, then that’s kind of a wrong note. But that’s not to say that you can play unintended notes that don’t lead you down another path that really opens up something else that you weren’t even thinking of when that note occurred.
I have a little quote here from Bill Dobbins, who I know you know who Bill Dobbins is.
Absolutely.
He said, “An essential part of real musicianship as an improviser or composer is the ability to use any note on the chromatic scale on any chord and make it sound believable.”

I think that’s a great quote, I mean and Bill can do that himself. I mean he’s an incredible musician and educator as well. Yeah I totally agree with that, and certain people are so fluid at it. I was listening to a Michael Brecker record a few days ago and I’m like what is he playing on that. And it’s like he’s playing a major third on a minor chord and it sounds like a million bucks. And I don’t know exactly why that’s working like that — but I mean I kind of know why it is but certain players just have that ability to basically what Bill — you quoted Bill as saying, and that’s basically playing any note on any chord and making it sound good.
Yeah. Miles Davis — you know something about with his Harmon mute it’s almost like he could play anything and somehow it’s like, “Yeah that’s great.”

I totally agree with you. I totally agree with that. And the beauty in his sound also helps a lot to make it — you know I think the Harmon is such a great sound the way he played it. And I think having a sound that you really love listening to makes those notes that maybe are outside of the chord center, makes those easier to listen to.
I can’t let this go by — I’m picturing you calling your mother saying, “Mom I’m leaving Eastman to go with Buddy Rich.” “Who’s Buddy Rich?” Did she know who Buddy Rich was?

She knew who Buddy Rich was, yeah, yeah. But yeah I mean the thing is I went to Eastman because they had a history of placing trombone players on Woody Herman’s band, especially like ten years before me, like for instance Jim Pugh and Birch Johnson and all these guys that I really looked up to and still do. And they were — it was kind of a pipeline there for a little bit so I thought well that’s the place that I should go. And as it turns out I ended up — I did play with Woody for a little bit but most of my big band time was with Buddy Rich. But it was a good pipeline and I knew when I got the call that this call might not happen again and I can always come back and finish my degree, which I did, and quite honestly a degree in trombone performance — an undergraduate degree in trombone performance is not very valuable in terms of the piece of paper. The © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

experience — extremely valuable. I mean it’s not like a music education degree where you can plug that into a work environment that you can get a job at. So it’s about — it’s like what we talked about at the beginning, the freelancing thing. It’s giving you the tools to be able to be a freelance musician. So I just thought this makes sense to me to take this. I understand it from my mom’s perspective. But she ended up being quite supportive about it so it all worked out in the end.
Did the fellas in the Buddy Rich band sort of band together to — I can’t finish my sentence.

I know where you’re going with this. Yeah. A hundred percent. Yeah it was kind of a us against him kind of vibe. And not always, and you know there’s all these tapes of him screaming, yelling at the band, and I was on several of those. But he wasn’t like that every day. You know it was, eh, a couple of times a month or something like that if I were to break it down, he’d get just really in a bad mood and take it out on the band a little bit. And during those periods it would definitely be kind of us against him. But other times he could be — he was a super funny guy when he wanted to be and he could kind of wrap his arms around us so to speak and include people on things. But I would say it was certainly a 50/50 situation — it was 50% of the time it was us against him.
And what about, let’s see Buddy Rich, Rolling Stones, Frank Sinatra?
Yeah.
Couldn’t play with anybody good, ey?

Yeah, I’m grateful for all the opportunities I’ve had. It’s been a terrific run. And if somebody would have told me 42 years ago when I got out of Eastman, “Here’s what you’re going to do would you take it right now?” I would take it in a heartbeat. And Sinatra was awesome. I mean when I started I was kind of the young guy on the band and the older guys who had been there for a long time, most of which are passed on now, they were really super great to me. They took me under their wing and the stories were incredible. And also that book of music to me is — there’ll never be a collection of arrangements that good again. Because not to say there aren’t great arrangers because there certainly are, but every one of those, you know when Sinatra picked up the phone so to speak, you know those arrangers brought their A game to the highest degree. So whether you’re playing a Billy May chart or a Nelson Riddle chart, which Nelson was probably the most associated with Frank, or Johnny Mandel, or Gordon Jenkins or Don Costa. These — they were all — every chart is a 10. And so for me as a young person getting to play that book, I loved every minute of it. It was awesome and you’re just hearing these absolute gems. You can’t play it wrong. You know you might crack a note but the figures are so beautifully constructed and the voicings and everything, it’s just everything was exactly the way you’d want to do it. And all of these — they were such © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

— well the arrangements still exist — they’re just such absolute gems. And so it’s unlikely that there would be a big band that would have that many different arrangers with different styles but all be that great. So it was a very special book of music to get to play on a nightly basis.
Yeah, to sit and be in the middle of that and realize the skill it took to know what not to write as well as what to write.

Yeah. Hundred percent. And you know I mean the one — Nelson Riddle comes to mind — I mean such a great arranger. And you know he was a trombone player, not a particularly great trombone player, but he was a trombone player, typically playing in a big band section, probably playing third trombone. And the way he learned how to write was he would write on little pieces of — you know like a single stave — and just write out some voicings. And he would get done with a rehearsal and just ask the guys to stick around for a couple of minutes and just play a couple of things. That’s how he learned how to arrange. You know there were no arranging books then or opportunities for him to try it. So he totally — he was sitting in the band and had obviously great ears and was listening to everything and figuring out okay how should I voice this, and what works good here, and you know all the different techniques that the great arrangers use. But he just figured them out by — very organically. So, and I’m sure many of the other arrangers same thing. But I know that story about Nelson for fact because people talk about it quite often.
You were horn-mates with Tim Ries is that correct?
That’s correct, yeah.
Here’s a quote, when I spoke to him about the Rolling Stones he said, “You get to know their kids and grandkids and wives, it’s like a big traveling family.”

Yeah they’re great people to work for. I loved how they treated the band — terrific. You know they could very easily have been off to themselves, the four Stones and just dealt with the upper level management, but they treated the band, we all flew on the same private plane with them. We always stayed at the same hotels with them and they treated you like you were a band you know. And obviously Keith and Mick and Charlie and Ron are more important than the saxophone player or the trombone player, but they viewed it like everybody was of value to them and they acted and treated us accordingly. Yeah, extremely grateful in many respects the best job I’ve ever had. But on the other hand there’s other factors involved in it too but they were terrific to work for.
I assume that they gave you a lot of notice when they were going to do a tour so that you could free up your calendar?

Yeah. And typically back then — I haven’t been with them for a number of years — but back then I was with them for about fifteen years, they were long tours. They’d be like a © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

year. The last one that I did spanned two years for a couple of different reasons. But you knew, they would give you a contract and you would be — it would be typically about a year. But like I said, sometimes longer. But yeah, they give you notice and every aspect of their approach to running the operation was so professional. It was really easy. You’ve got to just get up and make it to the lobby, and everything else will take care of itself.
Do you remember that quote from Charlie Watts about you?
I do, yeah.
Do you mind saying it for me?

Well yeah, he said, “In this bone dry era it’s essential to have Michael Davis around.” It’s not so applicable anymore ‘cause there’s so many great trombone players now that, I mean it’s never been healthier for the trombone in terms of the players that are playing now from Marshall Gilkes to Michael Dease to Ryan Keberle to just endless number — it feels like it’s endless. But back when I was starting and starting to do my own records, not as much. You know there weren’t as many trombone players around doing their own solo things so I think that’s why he may have said that. It was very kind of him and probably a little too generous. But I appreciated it of course. And he was a prince of a guy. I mean he was just a total gentleman. He was the anti rock star rock star. Because he would get done with a gig, he’d go to his room, maybe order some room service, go to bed, that’s it. And he didn’t want to be — I think he really didn’t like doing interviews, he didn’t really want to do — he was very kind of — but absolutely hysterical guy. I mean the driest sense of humor, it was terrific. So fun to hang out with. And as you know I’m sure, massive jazz fan, so he would always bring in — my trumpet colleague and I are very good friends still and we’d always sit next to each other on the plane and Charlie would come in and, “Look what I just bought, this is Elvin Jones’ drumset.” And it was like he was so happy. Like that made him much happier than whatever amount of money he was making that week being one of the Rolling Stones. So it was great, I mean he was just so much fun to talk to and hang out with, and a very approachable guy.

Okay I’m going to try a little something on you here. I have a list of some of the people that you’ve recorded for or perhaps done a tour with. And I’m going to start reading it and I want you to stop me if there’s something of significance that you’d like to say about it. All right?
Awesome.
Michael Jackson, Bob Dylan, Aerosmith —
Okay I mean I can say something about all of these —
I bet you can. Yeah we’ve got six hours here so let’s get started.

about what he wants. People will kind of add their input in kind of an organic creative process.
Yeah that’s like going to graduate school when you get in those situations. Like you can learn what you had at Eastman but you’ve got to add your own ear and intuition.

A hundred percent. And you know there’s a personal dynamic too because you want to know how far you can add input. Because some people don’t really want much more than what they’re saying and you have to try to interpret that and translate it into working for the horns. Let’s talk about advice you might give to young musicians today. I believe this is a quote from you from a previous interview and you said, “The inclusion of musicians on everything from CDs to film soundtracks to television commercials and Broadway shows no longer feels like a given but more like a luxury.”

Wow. If I said that I agree with myself then. Yeah, it certainly is, and I think especially now with the whole development of AI and everything that’s coming, boy there’s — the advice I would have with that in mind is become as versatile as you can become so you can deal with a lot of things and for instance by that I mean of course whatever your primary thing is, in my case it’s playing the trombone, be as good as you can possibly be in your primary thing but then also add some other tools to your toolbox. Add arranging. Add composition. If you are technically proficient be good at operating Pro Tools. If you can use Finale and understand how to copy things that’s actually also valuable. And then on top of all that, just work on your people skills you know people that work are people that other people like to be around. And you know I think, Monk, it’s probably the same as a college professor is the same as — you know people like to be around the people that they like. And so if you can make it easy for them to like you, you know don’t create a lot of problems. Don’t impose your thoughts all the time. Find out when it’s appropriate to add a comment here or there. Know what it is to go into a section and be playing third trombone and the lead trombone player has been there for 25 years and has a way of operating the section and just try to fit into that. If you have the ability to do that you’re © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

going to work a lot more for sure. And all those things I mean I think — I always say when I give clinics it’s like you’re opening a flower shop and there’s already five or six flower shops within a couple mile radius of you. So that’s not to say that you can’t be successful, but what’s going to make you more successful? So you know, oh that person always opens at 8:15 but it says 8:00 and, you know I hate going there because their person is always late and I need to get in and out of there so I can go to work or whatever analogy you want to use, all of those things factor in to somebody getting a call and I think now especially. The music business has always been a difficult business and it was challenging when I first started freelancing in New York, but it’s harder now and there’s less recording work, there’s less of the higher end kind of work. There’s still some, but it’s less and the level of players I would say is generally going up. So basically I’m saying the competition is even greater. Other things I would just add, just from a personal standpoint with my son Cole, who I had mentioned earlier who wrote “Open City,” he’s really developed his own Patreon channel like focusing on teaching and he does a Transcription Tuesday and he does a Monday Morning Warm-up session. He’s a bass player. And he’s gotten hundreds and hundreds of subscribers in about a year’s time and he’s really turned it into — it’s financially successful. So he figured out a way to use that tool — Patreon — and turn it into something that works for him and it enables him to use his skills in a way that can be profitable. So anything you could do like that — I’m sure there’s stuff that I’m not even aware of or have the ability to do that younger folks would take to quite naturally.

Well said. I want to talk about compositional inspiration for a moment. I was looking at your catalogue and I’m assuming these are your tunes or maybe your son’s. That’s very generous of me to describe that that way.
So what inspires a melodic line for you? Where does it start?

I’m not sure where it starts. I mean I think there’s a couple different approaches that I use and one is melody based, you know where the first thing that you come up with is a melody that anybody could — you just have something in your head and it could be a fragment of something else you’d heard that day, it could be — it could come from anywhere. It could be oh I had MLB network on and they had this like goofball theme and like for some reason it stuck in my head and then two weeks later you have something that resembles that or you know, whatever it might be, it just kind of comes out organically. melody in on top of that. And then kind of the third way would be dealing with the rhythmic element first and that’s going to create a different approach to how you’re going to write the melody. So I think I just kind of roll with whatever happens on that. The two tunes that you are referencing, “Life Lived” is a composition for six trombones that I wrote for a record I did called “New Brass.” And yeah, it’s exactly, it was a dedication to victims of 9/11. So you know that kind of has an implication about what kind of music that’s going to be. It’s kind of somber and in memoriam of that horrible day. “Stomper” is — I wanted to do something on a record I did called “Absolute Trombone II” that was for six trombones and drums. So that gives you a different kind of, you know, conjures up something else, like the music from “Life Lived” wouldn’t work well with the title “Stomper.”

Bob Mintzer told me once, I took some lessons from him before I was in his band, for composition and arranging. Yeah a hundred percent, yeah. And sometimes to the point of I want it to leave my head and I can’t get it out of my head. And then of course there’s the — you’re committed to it and you’ve done it all and it’s still in your head and you realize oh I wish I had done something different. That’s often part of the equation. So I find it to be a pretty frustrating process to be honest with you Monk, composition in general. And you hear these great songwriters talk about it from Billy Joel to Sting to Carla Bley, you know all range of styles. And a lot of them say the same thing you know and you’re writing and writing and then it’s just terrible so you throw it away and you start again and you just wasted the whole day.
